title: Omega Symbol: Copy & Paste Ω ω — And the Ohm Sign It's Often Confused With
meta_description: Copy and paste the Greek letter omega (Ω ω) and learn why the electrical ohm sign (U+2126) looks identical but is a different Unicode character — a real, documented source of bugs. Click any symbol to copy it instantly.
hero_tagline: The last letter of the Greek alphabet (Ω, ω) — and the reason the electrical ‘ohm’ sign for resistance looks exactly the same on screen while being a completely different Unicode character underneath. Click any symbol to copy it instantly.
intro: Omega (Ω uppercase, ω lowercase) is the 24th and final letter of the Greek alphabet — the source of ‘omega’ meaning ‘the end’ (as in the New Testament's ‘Alpha and Omega,’ Revelation 22:13), and the letter behind angular velocity (ω) and solid angle (Ω) in physics. It's also at the center of a genuine Unicode quirk: the electrical symbol for the ohm (resistance) has its own separate codepoint, U+2126 OHM SIGN, which Unicode's own official character list marks as normalizing to — and ‘preferred’ as — plain Greek omega (U+03A9). The two are supposed to be treated as the same character, but often aren't. Real bugs have followed: a documented Pandoc conversion issue handled the two inconsistently, converting one to LaTeX's \Omega while failing outright on the other, and electronics forums regularly discuss the two glyphs rendering slightly differently depending on font and OS.
